if: condition
introduces a possible situation and what follows from it
typical: if + present tense for the future, e.g. If you finish early... Also for general facts. NOT for: asking an indirect question (use 'whether').
If you finish early, you can leave.
We'll miss the train if we don't hurry.
If the door is locked, call me.
polite request
makes a request, offer or suggestion sound more polite
typical: spoken, e.g. I was wondering if you could... NOT for: describing a real condition.
I was wondering if you could lend me a pen.
Do you mind if I sit here?
It would help if you could arrive early.
advice
gives advice by imagining yourself in the other person's place
typical: spoken, e.g. If I were you, I'd... NOT for: talking about a real situation that you are in.
If I were you, I'd ask for a refund.
I'd take a coat if I were you.
If I were you, I'd call her today.
feelings
says how you feel about a possible situation, often to apologise or show you are open to it
typical: spoken, e.g. I'm sorry if I upset you. NOT for: a real condition with a result (see 'condition').
I'm sorry if I woke you.
I'm happy if everyone enjoys the party.
She doesn't mind if people disagree with her.
in addition: adds one more piece of information to what you have just said
typical: formal writing and presentations, at the start of a sentence. NOT for: contrast, or everyday speech where 'also' or 'and' is more natural.
The course is cheap. In addition, it can be done online.
The company offers free lunch. In addition, staff get extra holiday days.
She speaks Czech and English. In addition, she is learning Polish.
in any case: says that something will be true whatever happens
typical: spoken and written, at the start of a sentence or after 'but'. NOT for: a choice between two things.
I may be late, but in any case, start without me.
We might lose, but in any case, we'll have tried.
It will probably rain, but we're going in any case.
adds a further reason that makes the first point less important
typical: after a first reason, often with 'and' or at the start of a sentence. NOT for: contrasting two different facts.
I can't afford a new laptop, and in any case the old one still works.
He is too busy to help, and in any case he isn't good at it.
It's too late to call her now. In any case, I wouldn't know what to say.
in brief: introduces a short summary of what you have said or are going to say
typical: at the start of a sentence or between commas, formal or neutral. NOT for: leaving out important details when the person needs them.
In brief, the plan is cheap but risky.
The results, in brief, show that the method works.
In brief: we need more time and more money.
in contrast: introduces a second fact that is clearly different from the first one
typical: at the start of a sentence or between commas, writing and careful speech. NOT for: a surprising fact (use 'however').
The weekdays were quiet. In contrast, the weekends were very busy.
Sales fell in Europe. In contrast, they rose in Asia.
The first plan was simple. The second, in contrast, was very complicated.
compares one thing directly with another by using 'to' or 'with'
typical: in contrast to/with + noun phrase, e.g. in contrast to last year. NOT for: connecting two full sentences (use 'in contrast,').
In contrast to last year, this summer has been cold.
In contrast with his brother, he is very quiet.
The new design looks modern in contrast to the old building.
in essence: says what the most basic and important part of something is
typical: neutral to formal, introducing the main idea of an argument or belief. NOT for: adding a detail or giving an example.
In essence, the contract gives us more control.
The argument is, in essence, that taxes should be lower.
In essence, nothing has changed since last year.
in light of: says that you do or decide something after considering a particular fact or event
typical: formal; in British English usually 'in the light of', in American English 'in light of'. NOT for: talking about physical light.
In light of the new figures, we have changed our forecast.
The school closed early in the light of the storm warning.
In light of recent events, security has been increased.
in other words: says the same idea again in different, usually simpler, words
typical: spoken and written, after a complicated or indirect statement. NOT for: adding a new point or giving an example.
The shop closes at six. In other words, we have only an hour.
He never answers my messages. In other words, he doesn't want to talk.
The plan failed; in other words, we must start again.
in particular: points to one person, thing or part that matters more than the others
typical: after a general statement, at the end of a clause or at the start of a sentence. NOT for: a general list of examples (use 'for example').
The museum is wonderful, and the medieval section in particular.
The city has many parks. In particular, the old garden is worth a visit.
Please be careful, in particular on the stairs.
in practice: says what really happens, as opposed to what should happen or what people expect
typical: often after a rule or plan, e.g. in theory..., but in practice... NOT for: a repeated activity to improve a skill (the noun 'practice').
The rule says everyone must wear a helmet, but in practice few people do.
On paper the system is simple; in practice it is confusing.
In practice, most students never use the library's online tools.
in the end: says what finally happened after a long time, a process or some doubt
typical: spoken and written, at the start or end of a clause. NOT for: the end of a place or period (use 'at the end of') or the last item in a list (use 'finally').
We argued for an hour, but in the end we agreed.
I thought about studying law, but in the end I became a teacher.
It was a long trip, but in the end we reached the village.
insofar as: limits a statement by saying how far it is true
typical: formal, also written 'in so far as' or 'in as far as'. NOT for: distance (as in 'as far as the station').
The plan is acceptable insofar as it respects our budget.
Insofar as I can tell, the figures are correct.
She is guilty only insofar as she kept silent.
instead: says what happens or is done in place of the thing you have just mentioned
typical: at the start of a sentence or at the end of a clause. NOT for: use before a noun (use 'instead of').
I didn't take the bus. Instead, I walked home.
She didn't reply to the email. Instead, she called him.
The cinema was closed, so we went to a café instead.
it follows that: says that something must be true as a result of something else that is true
typical: formal arguments, often 'it does not follow that...'. NOT for: the order of events in time (use 'then' or 'after that').
If all students must attend, it follows that the room must be larger.
If the data are wrong, it follows that the conclusion is wrong too.
He owns the car, but it doesn't follow that he can drive it.
